name: Neutron
info: An atomic nucleus, or a [em1]nuclide[em1], is made of [em2]protons[em2] and [em3]neutrons[em3]. Protons have a positive charge to counteract the negative charge of [em2]electrons[em2] that orbit in shells around the nucleus. Neutrons have [em3]zero[em3] [em3]charge[em3]; that is to say they are neutral.[br] [br]More neutrons in a nucleus do not change an element's chemical properties but they do make it [em1]heavier[em1] and they can affect how [em2]stable[em2] the nuclide is. Nuclides that are not stable [em2]decay[em2] into other nuclides. The measure for how long a given nuclide will last is called its [em3]half-life[em3]. Nuclides decay [em1]at random[em1] so it's impossible to know exactly when a particular nuclide will decay. Instead, how long it takes about half of a bunch of the same nuclide to decay is measurable, and that's what half-life means.[br] [br]The nuclide that is a lone free neutron, [link]Neutron-1[link], has a half-life of about 10 minutes. This means if you had 1000 free neutrons then after ten minutes you could expect to have only 500, and only 250 left after 20 minutes. Neutrons are stable when combined with one or more protons to form an [em1]atomic nucleus[em1].

name: Hydrogen
info: As the very first element [em3]Hydrogen[em3] has only one proton. It's not just first on the Periodic Table, though, it's literally [em1]the first element to exist[em1]. To this day [em2]75% of all the matter in the universe is Hydrogen[em2].[br] [br]Hydrogen on its own is usually a [em1]gas[em1]. The two H's in [em3]H[sub]2[sub]0[em3] are the two Hydrogen atoms, combined with one Oxygen atom, to make [em2]water[em2]. In many common reactions between [em1]acids (like vinegar - C[sub]2[sub]H[sub]4[sub]O[sub]2[sub])[em1] and [em2]bases[em2] [em2](like baking soda - NaHCO[sub]3[sub])[em2], the acid gives a Hydrogen to the base.[br] [br]Hydrogen has two stable isotopes: [link]Hydrogen-1[link] with zero neutrons, also called [em3]Protium[em3], and [link]Hydrogen-2[link] with one neutron, also called [em3]Deuterium[em3] (remember: the number comes from the sum of neutrons and protons). With two neutrons, [link]Hydrogen-3[link] also has a special name: [em3]Tritium[em3]. Tritium has a [em1]half life[em1] of 12.32 years, making it the most stable [em1]radioisotope[em1] of Hydrogen (isotopes that are [em2]radioactive[em2] and decay). All the other isotopes of Hydrogen are very unstable and have half-lives that are only fractions of a second.

name: Helium
info: [em3]Helium[em3] is the lightest [em2]noble gas[em2], meaning it is both incredibly light and very non-reactive. In fact, to make [em1]compounds[em1] with Helium and other elements, it usually requires extreme temperatures or pressures.[br] [br]While Helium is the [em2]second most abundant[em2] element in the universe after [link]Hydrogen[link] it is somewhat rare on Earth because it is so light and non-reactive that it tends to float up to the top of the atmosphere and [em2]escape to space[em2]. Helium also has the lowest [em1]boiling point[em1] of any element, meaning its liquid state is incredibly cold [em2](around 4.2 K, or ​−452° F / −269° C)[em2]. This makes liquid Helium ideal for applications that require extremely low temperatures, such as the [em3]superconducting magnets[em3] used in MRI machines, particle accelerators, and quantum computers.[br] [br]When an atomic nucleus decays by [em3]Alpha (α) decay[em3] it emits an Alpha particle, composed of two [em1]neutrons and two protons[em1]... the same thing as a [link]Helium-4[link] nucleus. This reduces the parent nucleus atomic number by two, for example turning [link]Uranium-238[link] into [link]Thorium-234[link] + [link]Helium-4[link].

name: Boron
info: [em3]Boron[em3] has five protons and isn't made by [em1]fusion inside stars[em1]. Instead it comes from [em1]cosmic ray spallation[em1], where high-energy cosmic rays break apart heavier nuclei, and from supernovas. It's rare in the solar system and makes up only about [em2]0.001% of Earth's crust by weight[em2].[br] [br]Boron has two stable isotopes: [link]Boron-11[link] (about 80% of natural boron) and [link]Boron-10[link] (about 20%). Boron-10 has a high [em2]cross-section for neutron capture[em2], meaning it's very good at [em3]absorbing neutrons[em3]. That makes boron useful in nuclear reactors, in control rods and boric acid, for fission control and emergency shutdown.[br] [br]The same property is used in medicine. In [em1]boron neutron capture therapy[em1], a Boron-10 compound is taken up by a tumor and hit with low-energy neutrons. Each capture releases an alpha particle (a [link]Helium-4[link] nucleus) and a [link]Lithium-7[link] ion, which travel only a short distance, so the damage stays close to the tumor cells.[br] [br]Boron-11 is also a candidate fuel for [em1]aneutronic fusion[em1], a kind of fusion that produces few neutrons. Hit by a proton of about 500 keV, it produces [em3]three alpha particles[em3] and [em3]8.7 MeV of energy[em3].

name: Nitrogen
info: [em3]Nitrogen[em3] is one of the most common elements in the universe. Two atoms of it bond to form diatomic Nitrogen gas (N[sub]2[sub]), which makes up [em2]78% of Earth's atmosphere[em2].[br] [br]Nitrogen occurs in all organisms, primarily in [em1]amino acids[em1] (and thus proteins), in the [em1]nucleic acids (DNA and RNA)[em1] and in the energy transfer molecule [em1]adenosine triphosphate (ATP)[em1] that powers all cells. The human body contains about 3% nitrogen by mass. Because of its importance for life Nitrogen is a key component of [em2]fertilizers[em2], usually in the form of [em2]Ammonia (NH[sub]3[sub])[em2][br] [br]Nitrogen has many industrial applications. Due to its abundance, [em3]low boiling point (−195°C / −320°F)[em3], and low rate of evaporative loss [em3]liquid nitrogen[em3] is commonly used for cooling things to very low temperatures. This can include [em2]cryotherapies[em2] such as removing skin cysts and warts, [em2]cryopreservation[em2] of biological materials, and cooling sensitive electronics such as [em2]infrared and x-ray detectors[em2].

name: Scandium
info: [em3]Scandium[em3] has 21 protons and one stable isotope, [link]Scandium-45[link], so all natural scandium is the same nuclide. It was made in [em1]supernova explosions[em1] and by cosmic rays breaking apart heavier nuclei. It's about as common in Earth's crust as [link]Cobalt[link], but it's rarely concentrated and mostly comes as a [em2]byproduct of mining[em2].[br] [br]The world makes only about [em2]15 to 20 metric tons[em2] of scandium a year, but it's put to good use. Adding just a little to [link]Aluminium[link] makes a [em1]stronger alloy[em1] that has been used in Russian MiG fighter jets, baseball bats, bicycle frames, and lacrosse sticks. Scandium is also used in [em3]metal-halide lamps[em3], which make a white light close enough to sunlight for TV cameras to capture good color.[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Scandium-46[link], with a half-life of about 84 days, is used as a [em1]tracer in oil refineries[em1]. [link]Scandium-45[link] is even being studied for a [em2]nuclear clock[em2] that could, in theory, be far more precise than [link]Cesium[link] clocks.[br] [br]Scandium was found in 1879 by Swedish Chemist Lars Fredrik Nilson, and is named after [em3]Scandinavia[em3].

name: Vanadium
info: [em3]Vanadium[em3] has 23 protons, and nearly all natural vanadium (over 99%) is [link]Vanadium-51[link]. The other small percentage is [link]Vanadium-50[link], which is technically radioactive but has a half-life of 2.7 quintillion years, so it's [em1]effectively stable[em1].[br] [br]Vanadium has a moderate neutron-capture cross-section, and the isotopes it forms under neutron exposure have short half-lives, so it's considered a suitable material for the [em2]inner structure of a fusion reactor[em2].[br] [br]About 85% of Vanadium is used as an additive that [em2]significantly increases the strength of steel[em2]. The first large-scale industrial use was in the chassis of the [em1]Ford Model T[em1], and Vanadium steel is also used in axles, bicycle frames, crankshafts, and gears. It strengthens [link]Titanium[link] alloys for jet engines too, and [em3]Vanadium redox batteries[em3] are used for grid energy storage.[br] [br]It was named for Vanadís, another name for the [em3]Norse goddess Freyja[em3], because of its colorful compounds. Sea squirts are known to concentrate Vanadium in their blood cells.

name: Iron
info: [em3]Iron[em3] is a widely used metal that's the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. Extracting usable metal from ores containing Iron requires kilns or furnaces capable of reaching 1,500°C (2,730°F), about 500°C (900°F) higher than that required to smelt [link]Copper[link]. Humans first developed this technology around 4,000 years ago, leading to the [em2]Iron Age[em2].[br] [br]Iron is the [em1]heaviest element created by stellar fusion[em1]. Inside the core of stars fusing lighter elements to make heavier ones releases net energy, but Iron is the first element that when fused consumes energy. All elements heavier than Iron are either produced in [em3]supernova explosions[em3] or by means other than stellar fusion.[br] [br]Iron regularly forms various compounds with [link]Oxygen[link]. When metals [em1]rust[em1] it is the Iron combining with Oxygen to form [em3]Iron(III) Oxide (Fe[sub]2[sub]O[sub]3[sub])[em3]. The same affinity for Oxygen is why human blood is red; Iron in [em2]Hemoglobin[em2] is how red blood cells hold Oxygen for delivery to cells all around the body.

name: Rhodium
info: [em3]Rhodium[em3] has 45 protons and only one stable isotope, [link]Rhodium-103[link], which makes up 100% of natural rhodium. It's one of the [em1]rarest elements in Earth's crust[em1] with less than one part per billion. The world produces only about 30 metric tons a year, mostly in South Africa.[br] [br]About 80% of it goes into [em1]catalytic converters[em1], where Rhodium helps [em2]reduce nitrogen oxide emissions[em2]. Its price has swung from under $700 per troy ounce in 2016 to nearly $30,000 in 2021.[br] [br]Rhodium also has a job in nuclear power. [em2]Rhodium neutron detectors[em2] measure neutron flux levels in reactors, and each of the three reactors at Palo Verde has over 300 of them to give a [em2]3D picture of reactivity[em2]. Rhodium is also a [em1]fission product[em1] of [link]Uranium-235[link], but recovering it from used fuel is complex and expensive.[br] [br]Rhodium is [em3]electroplated[em3] onto white [link]Gold[link] and [link]Platinum[link] jewelry for a reflective finish. It was discovered in 1803 by English chemist William Hyde Wollaston and named from the Greek [em3]rhodon[em3], 'rose', for the color of one of its compounds.

name: Dysprosium
info: [em3]Dysprosium[em3] has 66 protons and [em1]seven stable isotopes[em1], led by [link]Dysprosium-164[link] at about 28% of the natural total. It's also very good at [em2]absorbing neutrons[em2], so mixtures of [em3]Dysprosium Oxide (Dy[sub]2[sub]O[sub]3[sub])[em3] and [link]Nickel[link] are used as control rods in nuclear reactors.[br] [br]But dysprosium is best known for its [em1]magnets[em1]. Replacing a bit of the [link]Neodymium[link] in neodymium magnets with dysprosium (up to 6%) helps them keep their magnetism in demanding uses like [em3]electric vehicle motors[em3] and [em3]wind turbine generators[em3]. An electric car can contain up to 100 grams of it.[br] [br]Dysprosium and [link]Holmium[link] have the highest magnetic strengths of any elements, especially at low temperatures. Dysprosium is also in [em2]Terfenol-D[em2], an alloy that changes shape in a magnetic field more than any other known material at room temperature, and is used in [em1]transducers and fuel injectors[em1].[br] [br]Its name comes from the Greek for [em3]'hard to get'[em3] as its discoverer, French chemist Paul Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, needed more than 30 attempts to separate it.

name: Iridium
info: [em3]Iridium[em3] has 77 protons and two stable isotopes: [link]Iridium-193[link] (about 63% of natural iridium) and [link]Iridium-191[link] (about 37%). It's formed by rapid neutron capture in [em1]neutron star mergers[em1], and it's one of the least abundant elements in Earth's crust, though much more common in meteorites.[br] [br]That rarity is why a thin iridium-rich layer of clay at the boundary between the Cretaceous and Paleogene periods [em2]66 million years ago[em2] stood out. In 1980 a team led by American physicist Luis Alvarez proposed it came from space, and the idea that a [em3]meteor impact caused the extinction of the dinosaurs[em3] is now widely accepted.[br] [br]Radioactive [link]Iridium-192[link], with a half-life of about 74 days, is used in [em1]brachytherapy[em1] (a form of cancer radiotherapy) and industrial radiography. Iridium is the [em3]second-densest[em3] metal after [link]Osmium[link] and the [em3]most corrosion-resistant[em3] metal known, so it's used in spark plug electrodes and in crucibles for growing crystals. It's named for Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because its compounds have a [em2]variety of colors[em2].

name: Astatine
info: [em3]Astatine[em3] has 85 protons and [em1]no stable isotopes[em1]. The longest-lived, [link]Astatine-210[link], has a half-life of just 8.1 hours. The element's name comes from the [em2]Greek for 'unstable'[em2].[br] [br]That makes it [em3]the rarest naturally occurring element[em3]. Any Astatine present when the Earth formed is long gone, and the little that exists is constantly forming as a decay product of [link]Uranium[link] and [link]Thorium[link]. The entirety of the Earth's crust is estimated hold [em2]less than one gram[em2] at any given time.[br] [br]Astatine was first produced in 1940 at UC Berkeley by bombarding [link]Bismuth-209[link] with alpha particles ([link]Helium-4[link] nucleii) in a cyclotron. Today [link]Astatine-211[link], with a half-life of 7.2 hours, is being studied for [em1]targeted alpha-particle therapy[em1], though it has to be used quickly.[br] [br]No one has ever seen a solid sample of astatine, because any visible amount would be [em3]vaporized by the heat of its own radioactivity[em3]. It's the heaviest naturally occurring halogen, in the same group as [link]Iodine[link].

name: Protactinium
info: [em3]Protactinium[em3] has 91 protons and [em1]no stable isotopes[em1]. The longest-lived, [link]Protactinium-231[link], has a half-life of about 33,000 years, and it's found in nature because it is produced by the decay of naturally-occurring [link]Uranium-235[link].[br] [br]Its name comes from the Greek [em2]protos[em2], meaning 'first', because [link]Protactinium-231[link] decays into [link]Actinium[link].[br] [br]Protactinum also shows up in nuclear energy. In the [em1]thorium fuel cycle[em1], [link]Thorium-232[link] absorbs a neutron and eventually becomes [link]Protactinium-233[link], which decays into [link]Uranium-233[link]. But Protactinium-233 absorbs neutrons too, making it a [em2]neutron poison[em2], so it's removed from thorium reactors as they run.[br] [br]Protactinium is one of the [em1]rarest and most expensive[em1] natural elements, at just a few parts per trillion of the Earth's crust. In 1961, 127 grams of it were extracted from 60 metric tons of waste. It can also be used for [em3]radiometric dating[em3] of geologic sediments up to 175,000 years old.

name: Americium
info: [em3]Americium[em3] is a synthetic element that can be produced by [link]Uranium[link] or [link]Plutonium[link] being [em2]bombarded with neutrons in nuclear reactors[em2]. It was originally discovered as a part of the [em1]Manhattan Porject[em1] to build the first atomic bomb.[br] [br][em3]Smoke detectors[em3] work using Americium. About 0.29 micrograms of [em2]Americium Dioxide (AmO[sub]2[sub])[em2] regularly emits alpha particles ([link]Helium-4[link] nucleii) as the Americium decays to [link]Neptunium-237[link]. A detector measures the flow of ions across a gap, and when smoke enters that gap it [em1]absorbs the alpha particles[em1], triggering the alarm.[br] [br]The name of Americium was chosen to refer to the Americas as an analogy to the previously discovered [link]Europium[link], named for Europe, which is the next lighter element in the same [em2]periodic table group[em2].

name: Californium
info: [em3]Californium[em3] has 98 protons and is [em1]synthetic[em1]. [link]Californium-252[link] has a half-life of about 2.6 years, and roughly 3% of its decays are [em1]spontaneous fission[em1], making it a powerful neutron source: just one microgram emits about [em2]2.3 million neutrons per second[em2].[br] [br]That makes it useful as a startup neutron source for some nuclear reactors, for inspecting aircraft parts for cracks and corrosion, for finding water and oil layers in wells, and for portable [link]Gold[link] and [link]Silver[link] prospecting. Its neutrons are even used to treat some [em3]cervical and brain cancers[em3] where other radiation therapy is ineffective.[br] [br]Californium is [em1]extremely scarce[em1]. As of 2003 only two sites made [link]Californium-252[link], producing 0.25 grams a year at Oak Ridge and 0.025 grams a year in Russia.[br] [br]Californium was first made in 1950 in Berkeley, California by bombarding [link]Curium-242[link] with alpha particles ([link]Helium-4[link] nucleii), producing only about [em2]5,000 atoms[em2]. It's named after the University of California and the state. Decades later, [link]Californium-249[link] was the target used to make [link]Oganesson[link], the heaviest element made so far.

name: Nihonium
info: Discoverered at the [em1]RIKEN Nishina Center for Accelerator-Based Science[em1] in Japan, this element was officially named on June 8, 2016. The root of its name, [em3]Nihon[em3], is one of the two ways to say [em3]Japan[em3] in Japanese, literally meaning [em2]the Land of Rising Sun[em2]. Nihonium is the first element to be discovered by an Asian country.

name: Muscovium
info: Officially named on June 8, 2016, [em3]Muscovium[em3] is so named in recognition of the [em3]Moscow[em3] region. This honors the ancient Russian land that is the home of the [em1]Joint Institute for Nuclear Research[em1] where the discovery experiments were conducted using the [em2]Dubna Gas-Filled Recoil Separator[em2] in combination with the heavy ion accelerator capabilities of the [em2]Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions[em2].

name: Livermorium
info: [em3]Livermorium[em3] is an extremely radioactive element that has never been observed in nature. As of 2020 only [em2]35 individual atoms[em2] of Livermorium have been created in laboratories.[br] [br]The first synthesis of Livermorium was in 2000 when scientists at the [em1]JINR lab in Dubna, Russia[em1] bombarded [link]Curium-248[link] with accelerated ions of [link]Calcium-48[link], producing a single atom via [em2]nuclear fusion[em2] which quickly decayed to [link]Flerovium-289[link].[br] [br]As a particularly large nucleus its inner shell electrons have an incredibly high velocity, approaching the [em3]speed of light[em3]. Due to its short half life little has been confirmed for how Livermorium would behave chemically, but being in the same group as [link]Oxygen[link] and [link]Sulfur[link] suggest it could form [em1]Livermorium Hydride (H[sub]2[sub]Lv)[em1], a similar compound to [em2]hydrogen sulfide (H[sub]2[sub]S) or water (H[sub]2[sub]O)[em2].

name: Tennessine
info: Officially named on June 8, 2016, [em3]Tennessine[em3] is so named in recognition of the contributions of the [em3]Tennessee[em3] region of the United States to superheavy element research. This region is home to the [em1]Oak Ridge National[em1] [em1]Laboratory[em1], [em1]Vanderbilt University[em1], and the [em1]University of Tennessee at Knoxville[em1].

name: Oganesson
info: Officially named on June 8, 2016, [em3]Oganesson[em3] honors [em2]Professor Yuri Oganessian[em2] for his pioneering contributions to research of super heavy elements. Among many acheivements in the field he helped produce experimental evidence for the [em3]island of stability[em3].
